GRANTING BLM’s MOTION TO VACATE AND REMAND
DENYING WWP’s MOTION TO DISMISS WITH INSTRUCTIONS
DISMISSING APPEALS

ID-096-04-001 and -015
I. Introduction
Three environmental protection groups and a grazing permittee have appealed a decision
of the Owyhee (Idaho) Field Office, Bureau of Land Management. The decision renewed the
grazing permit for the Pole Creek Allotment under revised conditions. The matter is now before
me on (1) a Request for Vacation and Remand, filed by the BLM; and (2) a Motion to Dismiss
with Instructions, filed by Western Watersheds Project, Committee for the High Desert, and
Idaho Bird Hunters (“WWP”).
After review of the parties’ submissions I have determined that BLM’s motion should be
granted because BLM retains the discretion to vacate its own decision and that WWP’s motion
most be denied because an Administrative Law Judge lacks authority to impose conditions upon
BLM when an appeal is voluntarily dismissed. Further, since the appealed decision is vacated,
the appeals become moot and must be dismissed.
II. Procedural Background
The history of these appeals stems from the terms of a federal district court order
requiring the BLM to complete a review of several grazing allotments including the one subject
to these appeals. 1/ BLM timely issued its decision which extended the term of the permit for ten
years and imposed certain new conditions designed to improve rangeland health. WWP and the
permittee filed separate appeals under the Taylor Grazing Act. 2/ WWP claimed BLM violated
several environmental protection statutes. 3/ The permittee objected to the changed terms and
conditions of the permit. 4/ WWP also requested a stay, which the Board of Land Appeals
denied. 5/ I subsequently consolidated the appeals of WWP and the permittee and later
substituted Roy Hall for the original permittee when he purchased the grazing allotment.

Shortly before the hearing date BLM filed a request to vacate and remand its decision. 6/
WWP has opposed BLM’s motion, stating that it does not oppose BLM’s efforts to reverse and
remand the field office decision, but moving that conditions be attached to a dismissal. 7/ The
current permittee, Roy Hall, has not opposed BLM’s request to vacate and remand. 8/ He has
opposed WWP’s motion to dismiss with conditions but wants the conditions modified if the
motion is granted. 9/ I subsequently cancelled the hearing and took the motions under review.
III. Analysis
A. BLM’s Motion to Vacate and Remand
I first address BLM’s motion to vacate and remand. This motion should be granted
because an ALJ does not have authority to require BLM to adhere to a decision it no longer
supports. WWP has not cited any authority to deny BLM the right to vacate its own decision and
issue a new one, nor have I found any such authority in the statutes, regulations, or decisions of
the Board of Land Appeals. An ALJ should be guided by the principle that the Secretary has
granted BLM the authority to make initial grazing decisions. 10/ The Secretary has granted an
ALJ only the authority to consider an appeal of a grazing decision. 11/ An order refusing to allow
BLM to vacate its own decision would force BLM to adopt a decision it no longer desires to
make. 12/

ID-096-04-001 and -015
The recent unpublished decision of the Board in Petan Company of Nevada 13/ supports
this conclusion. In that case an ALJ had granted BLM’s motion to vacate a final multiple use
decision. The Board refused to “reverse the administrative law judge and compel him to conduct
a hearing on a decision BLM no longer wishes to implement.” It reasoned that the ALJ may
consider only decisions of agency officers and “[w]here BLM does not endorse its decision and
seeks to withdraw it, there is no BLM decision to consider.”14/
The only argument for requiring BLM to not vacate its decision may be inferred from
WWP’s motion supporting a dismissal with instructions. WWP argues that BLM is likely to
make the same alleged errors in a subsequent decision. 15/ While WWP may see a pattern of
unlawful conduct in BLM’s past decisions, the lawfulness of any future decisions must be left to
a later review. A conclusion today that BLM will violate the law in the future would be
speculation.
In granting BLM’s request to vacate and remand I expressly make no finding or
conclusion on what terms or conditions may govern future grazing on the allotment until BLM
issues a new decision. This issue is not now before me.
B. WWP’s Motion to Dismiss with Instructions
Having considered BLM’s motion, I turn to WWP’s motion to dismiss with instructions.
This motion must be denied because no authority exists for an ALJ to dismiss an appeal with
instructions and because reliance on federal court civil procedure rules for this authority would
not be appropriate.
An ALJ’s authority is derived from express grants from Congress or from the Secretary.
The regulations governing grazing procedure give authority for an ALJ to “make findings of fact
and conclusions of law * * * and render a decision upon all material issues of fact and law
presented on the record.” 16/ The regulations say nothing about authority to issue instructions to
BLM without having conducted a hearing and WWP has cited no regulations or statutes granting
such authority.

14/ Id., slip op. at 8.
15/ Appellant’s Opposition to BLM’s Motion to Vacate and Remand, and WWP’s
Motion to Dismiss with Instructions, dated May 8, 2006, at 2 and 5-10.
16/ 43 CFR 4.477(a) (2005).
4

ID-096-04-001 and -015
Rather, WWP argues that Rule 41(a)(2) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure provides
authority for an ALJ to dismiss with instructions to BLM. The simple response is that these rules
apply only to proceedings in a federal district court. Because WWP’s appeal is before an office
of the Department of the Interior, an agency in the executive branch of government, the rules of
the judicial branch do not apply.
Even if the judicial rules applied, or could be followed by analogy, Rule 41(a)(2) would
not authorize the instructions that WWP seeks. The general purpose of Rule 41(a)(2) is to
“preserve a plaintiff’s right to take a voluntary nonsuit and start over so long as the defendant is
not hurt.” 17/ Under this rule, terms and conditions may not be imposed upon the non-moving
party. 18/ Because BLM is the non-moving party, the rule does not permit imposition of terms
and conditions binding on BLM.
Further, subjecting BLM to binding instructions would be equivalent to granting remedies
to WWP for a successful appeal. Remedies cannot be granted in this circumstance because
WWP has not proven that BLM committed error. 19/
WWP has cited an order of the Idaho District Court in Western Watersheds Project v.
Secrist 20/ as precedent. This case dismissed WWP’s action against BLM with instructions that
BLM not implement a challenged settlement agreement, that BLM complete a new NEPA
analysis and that BLM issue a new grazing decision. Again the simple response is that the order
is not relevant because it applies a federal court rule that is not binding in this administrative
proceeding. Further, the court order appears to rely upon representations made by BLM that it
would do what the order instructed. 21/ BLM has made no such representations in this

administrative appeal. Thus, even if the federal court rules applied, the case would be of
minimal precedential value.
IV. Conclusion
Having taken the motions under review it is now ordered that:
1. The Request for Vacation and Remand filed by the Bureau of Land Management is
granted.
2. The Decision of the Field Office Manager, Owyhee Field Office, Lower Snake River
District, Bureau of Land Management, dated September 3, 2003, related to the Pole Creek
Allotment, is vacated.
3. Further consideration of the grazing permit for the Pole Creek Allotment is remanded
to the Bureau of Land Management.
4. The Motion to Dismiss with Instructions filed by appellants Western Watersheds
Project, Committee for the High Desert, and Idaho Bird Hunters is denied.
5. The appeals filed by Western Watersheds Project, Committee for the High Desert,
Idaho Bird Hunters, Roy Hall (as successor in interest to Lazaro Mendieta) and Circle Bar
Ranches LLC (Case Nos. ID-096-04-001 and ID-096-04-015) are dismissed as moot.
Right of Appeal
Any party adversely affected by this decision has the right to appeal to the Interior Board
of Land Appeals. The appeal must comply strictly with the regulations in 43 CFR Part 4.
Selected provisions of these regulations are attached.
